parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: An electromagnetic wave in a vacuum has a wavelength of $8.4 \times 10^{-6} \text{m}$.
parts.text: State the name of the principal region of the electromagnetic spectrum for the wave.
hints: Hint 1: Compare the given wavelength $8.4 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$ with visible light which is about $4$ to $7 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ - is it longer or shorter, and which region lies just beyond red light?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Place the Wavelength on the Spectrum**
Think of the spectrum in order of increasing wavelength: gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio. Visible red light ends at about $7 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Identify the Region**
Here $$\lambda = 8.4 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m} = 8400 \text{ nm}$$ which is about 10 times longer than red light but much shorter than microwaves ($\sim 10^{-2} \text{ m}$). This is the principal region of infrared.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the frequency, in THz, of the wave.
hints: Hint 1: All electromagnetic waves in vacuum travel at the same speed - recall the value of $c$ and how $c$, $f$ and $\lambda$ are linked.
Hint 2: After finding $f$ in $\text{Hz}$, remember $1 \text{ THz} = 10^{12} \text{ Hz}$, so divide by $10^{12}$ to convert to $\text{THz}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the Universal Wave Speed**
In vacuum every EM wave travels at $$c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$ The wave equation is $$c = f\lambda$$ so $$f = \frac{c}{\lambda}$$

Step 2: **Calculate and Convert**
Substitute values: $$f = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8}{8.4 \times 10^{-6}} = 3.57 \times 10^{13} \text{ Hz}$$ Since $1 \text{ THz} = 10^{12} \text{ Hz}$: $$f = \frac{3.57 \times 10^{13}}{10^{12}} \approx 36 \text{ THz}$$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
An arrangement that uses a double slit to demonstrate the interference of light from a laser is shown in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1 (not to scale)

The light from the laser has a wavelength of $6.2 \times 10^{-7} \text{m}$ and is incident normally on the slits. The separation of the two slits is $a$. The slits and screen are parallel and separated by a distance of $2.8 \text{m}$.

An interference pattern of bright fringes and dark fringes is formed on the screen. The distance on the screen across 8 bright fringes is $22 \text{mm}$, as illustrated in Fig. 5.2.

{{figure:figure_5_2}}

Fig. 5.2
parts.text:
The light waves emerging from the two slits are coherent.

State what is meant by coherent.

markscheme_points.text: constant phase difference (between the waves) (with time)

hints: Hint 1: For a clear stable fringe pattern the two sources must interfere in the same way all the time - what property of the two waves must therefore not change with time?
parts.proper_answer: Coherent means having a constant phase difference with time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why Coherence Matters**
Interference gives bright where waves arrive in phase and dark where they arrive in antiphase. If the phase relationship at the slits kept jumping around, the pattern would wash out.

Step 2: **Define Coherent**
Two waves are coherent when they have the same frequency and a constant phase difference with time. Laser light from the two slits satisfies this because both beams come from the same source.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the separation $a$ of the slits.
hints: Hint 1: Recall the double-slit formula linking wavelength $\lambda$, slit separation $a$, fringe spacing $x$ and slit-to-screen distance $D$.
Hint 2: The diagram shows 22 mm across 8 bright fringes - think carefully how to get the spacing $x$ between one adjacent pair, and convert it to metres.
Hint 3: Rearrange to make $a$ the subject and check all units are in metres before calculating.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write Down the Fringe Formula**
For double-slit interference: $$\lambda = \frac{ax}{D}$$ where $x$ is the fringe spacing (adjacent bright to adjacent bright), $a$ is slit separation and $D$ is slits to screen distance. So $$a = \frac{\lambda D}{x}$$

Step 2: **Find One Fringe Spacing x**
Do not use 22 mm as $x$. That is 8 spacings: $$x = \frac{22 \text{ mm}}{8} = 2.75 \text{ mm} = 2.75 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$$ Also $\lambda = 6.2 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ and $D = 2.8 \text{ m}$.

Step 3: **Calculate a**
$$a = \frac{(6.2 \times 10^{-7}) \times 2.8}{2.75 \times 10^{-3}}$$ $$a = 6.3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$$ This small sub-mm separation is typical for visible-light interference.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: Fringe P is the central bright fringe of the interference pattern in (b). Fringe Q and fringe R are the nearest dark fringe and the nearest bright fringe respectively to the right of fringe P, as shown in Fig. 5.2.
parts.text: Calculate the difference in the distances (the path difference) from each slit to the centre of fringe Q.
hints: Hint 1: Fringe Q is the first dark fringe next to the central bright fringe - recall the path-difference condition for destructive interference in terms of $\lambda$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply the Dark Fringe Condition**
At the central bright fringe P the path difference is zero. Moving out to the first dark fringe Q, the waves must cancel, so they arrive in antiphase. That needs a path difference of half a wavelength: $$\text{path difference} = \frac{\lambda}{2}$$

Step 2: **Calculate**
$$\text{path difference} = \frac{6.2 \times 10^{-7}}{2} = 3.1 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: State the phase difference between the light waves meeting at the centre of fringe R.
hints: Hint 1: Fringe R is a bright fringe, so the waves arrive in phase - what phase difference in degrees corresponds to constructive interference one full wavelength out from the centre?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Bright Fringe to Phase**
Fringe R is the first-order bright fringe. The path difference there is one full wavelength $\lambda$, so the waves reinforce and arrive in phase.

Step 2: **State the Phase Difference**
One full wavelength corresponds to one full cycle of phase: $$\text{phase difference} = 360^{\circ}$$ This is equivalent to $0^{\circ}$ or $2\pi \text{ rad}$, meaning fully in phase.
